ox: Incorrect. 9R is what you get if you divide the distance by 9 instead of the field: it forgets the SQUARE. At r = 9R, g = GM/(9R)² = GM/(81R²) = g₀/81, far weaker than one-ninth.
Incorrect. √3·R makes r² = 3R², so g = GM/(3R²) = g₀/3, only one-third. This choice takes a square root of the wrong number (3 instead of 9).
Incorrect. 81R squares the factor again. At r = 81R, g = g₀/6561. Squaring happens once, in g = GM/r²; do not square the answer a second time.
Correct. g = GM/r² and g₀ = GM/R². We want g = g₀/9, so r² = 9R², and r = 3R. Check: g = GM/(3R)² = GM/(9R²) = g₀/9. Remember r is measured from Earth's CENTER, so 3R is only 2R above the ground.

concept.t: Gravity versus distance: the inverse-square law
p: Newton's law says the pull of Earth on a small mass falls off as 1/r², where r is the distance to Earth's CENTER. Double the distance and the pull drops to 1/4; triple it and the pull drops to 1/9; ten times and it drops to 1/100.
So 'one-ninth' tells you immediately that the distance must have been multiplied by 3, because 3² = 9. Potential energy is different: U = −GMm/r goes as 1/r, so tripling r only cuts U to one-third.

x4A_094.trap: Answering 9R (forgetting the square) or 2R (height above the ground instead of distance from the center).
x4A_094.eli: Gravity is like a flashlight beam spreading out: at 3 times the distance the light covers 3 × 3 = 9 times the area, so every spot gets one-ninth as much light.
mem: r is measured from Earth's CENTER. r = 3R means only 2R above the surface.
Potential energy U = −GMm/r goes as 1/r (tripling r gives 1/3, not 1/9).

fm.f: g = G·M / r², where g = gravitational field strength at distance r, G = gravitational constant (never changes), M = mass of Earth, r = distance from Earth's CENTER
fm.v: At the surface r = R, so g₀ = G·M/R². We want g = g₀/9.
fm.why: We use g = GM/r² because gravity weakens with the distance SQUARED: farther away = weaker.

x4A_094.sc: Skip the algebra: 'one-ninth' means (distance factor)² = 9, so the distance factor is √9 = 3.
x4A_094.mn: Triple the distance, ninth the pull: r × 3 → g ÷ 9.

ox: Correct. A third-law pair is the same type of force acting on the OTHER object. Earth pulls the book down by gravity, so the book pulls Earth up by gravity with equal size.
Incorrect. The table's normal force on the book is equal and opposite to the weight only because the book is not accelerating. It acts on the SAME object (the book), so it is not a third-law partner.
Incorrect. The book's push on the table is the third-law partner of the table's normal force on the book, not of gravity.
Incorrect. 'The table's weight' is not a force on the book or related to this pair. Weight is Earth's pull on the table.

p: Newton's third law: if object A exerts a force on object B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A, of the SAME type. The two forces act on different objects. Weight (Earth on book) pairs with the book's gravitational pull on Earth; the normal force (table on book) pairs with the book's push on the table.

x4A_058.trap: Choosing the normal force because it is equal and opposite. A true pair also acts on DIFFERENT objects.
x4A_058.eli: If I push a wall, the wall pushes me back. If Earth pulls the book, the book pulls Earth.
mem: Third-law pairs: same type of force, equal size, opposite direction, on DIFFERENT objects.
Weight and normal force are NOT a pair (same object).
The pair of 'Earth pulls book' is 'book pulls Earth'.
x4A_058.sc: Swap the two names: 'Earth on book' → 'book on Earth'.
